newsitem.title: USA: EchoStar to honor News Corp deal.
newsitem.headline: EchoStar to honor News Corp deal.

text.p: EchoStar Communications Corp Chairman and Chief Executive Charles Ergen said Tuesday he plans to honor the agreement with News Corp Ltd in their direct-TV satellite venture.
On Monday, EchoStar had said it was delaying regulatory filings on the venture over demands by News Corp that EchoStar abandon the conditional-access system it currently uses.

At a satellite television conference in New York on Tuesday, Ergen said he still expects the venture to proceed despite the setback. Ergen also said that EchoStar is not having discussions with any other potential partners.
"I'm very hopeful...that this issue will not be a stumbling block," he said.
Later, Ergen told reporters, "The deal will go forward with News Corp."
The planned venture is to offer as many as 500 channels of digital TV, Internet services and local broadcast TV signals to market across the United States.
It is viewed as competition to DirecTV, which is owned by General Motors Corp's Hughes Electronics Corp and AT&T Corp and Primestar, a partnership of cable TV operators.
Ergen would not say how long the dispute with News Corp could delay a launch of the venture, or when regulatory filings would now be submitted.
"We don't have a timetable," he said.
A critical component of the direct-broadcast satellite industry is the conditional-access system, an encryption service that allows subscribers to view only those channels for which they have paid.
EchoStar currently uses a conditional-access system offered by Nagra SA, while News Corp owns another vendor called News Digital System.
Ergen said that, before considering a switch to News Corp's conditional-access system, he would need to make sure it fits the criteria outlined in their agreement.
"The heart of your system in DBS is you're conditional- access system," Ergen said during a panel discussion at the conference. "So it's critical to all of us...that the system is secure."
Ergen said EchoStar is seeking additional financial and technical information from News Corp of its conditional-access system.
Although it may be "technically feasible" to switch to News Corp's service, Ergen said he first wants to understand the financial and logistical implications.
Ergen said he has no contingency plan if the deal falls through and is not talking with potential partners.
For the past several months, EchoStar had been looking for financial partnerships since dropping the price of its satellite dishes.
Nevertheless, Ergen still believes the company pursued the right strategy by dropping its prices to $199, particularly since the company was a relatively new player to the industry.
"We thought that's where the marketplace was going to go," he said. "We figured we might as well bring it there."
"We thought that's where the marketplace was going to go," he said. "We figured we might as well bring it there."
Under the deal, EchoStar could request $200 million in financing from News Corp as of May 1 out of the $1 billion investment pledged by News Corp.
However, Ergen said he does not believe EchoStar will need that money right away.
"We'd only request it if we needed it," he told reporters. "It's not likely we'll need it May 1st."
Ergen, who founded the Denver-based company, said he also was not concerned about EchoStar's stock price, which hit a 52-week high of 36-1/2, but now rests at about 14-3/8.
"We're going to build long-term value," said Ergen, who owns 30 million shares of EchoStar.
Analysts said Ergen's remarks confirmed their belief that the venture will indeed proceed.
"I still say the deal makes sense for both companies and both are certainly worse off without the deal," Lazard Freres analyst John Hodulik said.
((-- Lisa Marie Pane, New York newsdesk 212-859-1713))
